questions.text: Which one of the following is a top-down parser?
questions.solution:
A recursive descent parser starts from the start symbol and expands it down to the input, so it is top-down. SLR and LR(k) are bottom-up.

Answer: Recursive descent parser

questions.text:
Which grammar rules violate the requirement of the operator grammar? A, B, C are variables and a, b, c are terminals
1. [latex]A \rightarrow B C[/latex]
2. [latex]A \rightarrow C c B b[/latex]
3. [latex]A \rightarrow B a C[/latex]
4. [latex]A \rightarrow \epsilon[/latex]
questions.solution:
An operator grammar has no [latex]\epsilon[/latex]-productions and no two adjacent non-terminals.

- 1: B C are adjacent [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] violates
- 4: [latex]\epsilon[/latex] [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] violates
- 2 and 3 have terminals between non-terminals [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] fine

Answer: 1 and 4

questions.text:
The number of tokens in the following C statement is
 printf("i=%d, &i=%x", i, &i);
questions.solution:
Tokens: printf, (, "i=%d, &i=%x", ",", i, ",", &, i, ), ;

The whole string literal is one token. Total = 10

Answer: 10

questions.text:
Given the following expression grammar:
[latex]E \rightarrow E * F|F+E| F[/latex]
[latex]F \rightarrow F-F \mid i d[/latex]
Which of the following is true?
questions.solution:
Operators lower in the grammar bind tighter. "[latex]-[/latex]" is produced by F (the lowest level), while * and + are produced by E.

So [latex]-[/latex] has higher precedence than * (and +).

Answer: [latex]-[/latex] has higher precedence than *

questions.text:
Consider the following grammar
S [latex] \rightarrow[/latex] F|H
F [latex] \rightarrow[/latex] p|c
H [latex] \rightarrow[/latex] d|c
where S,F, and H are non-terminal symbols, p,d, and c are terminal symbols. Which of the following statement(s) is/are correct?
S1. LL(1) can parse all strings that are generated using grammar G
S2. LR(1) can parse all strings that are generated using grammar G
questions.solution:
The string "c" has two derivations: [latex]S\Rightarrow F\Rightarrow c[/latex] and [latex]S\Rightarrow H\Rightarrow c[/latex]. So the grammar is ambiguous.

No ambiguous grammar is LL(1) or LR(1).

Answer: Neither S1 nor S2
